paragraphs: Minimax optimization involves variables with opposing goals: one side minimizes an objective while the other maximizes it. This paper develops a general acceleration framework for smooth objectives that are strongly convex on the minimizing side and concave on the maximizing side. Its contribution is a reusable scheme that builds on existing gradient algorithms.

The method has two nested loops. It applies Catalyst, an accelerated proximal point framework, to the associated dual problem. Within this outer procedure, existing algorithms solve a sequence of better-balanced problems that have both strong convexity and strong concavity. This organization lets the framework benefit from available solvers while improving the overall theoretical computational cost.

The authors establish a family of near-optimal algorithms and introduce variance-reduced versions for objectives with finite-sum structure, obtaining faster convergence. They also extend the approach to nonconvex-concave problems, where the target is a stationary point, and report state-of-the-art complexity for that setting. Numerical experiments support the framework’s practical benefits alongside its theoretical guarantees.
neurips-2020-a-catalyst-framework-for-mi.tldr: A two-loop Catalyst framework accelerates minimax optimization by wrapping existing gradient methods around a sequence of better-conditioned subproblems.

paragraphs: Neural network compression can reduce numerical precision or remove parts of a model. Bayesian Bits treats these decisions within one trainable framework, allowing different tensors to use different bit widths while also supporting pruning. The goal is to learn how much precision to retain through gradient-based optimization.

The method represents quantization as a sequence of refinements. It first rounds a full-precision value, then quantizes the remaining error at stages that double the bit width. Adding a refinement increases effective precision and reduces quantization noise. Starting from a power-of-two bit width produces hardware-friendly configurations, while an additional zero-bit choice incorporates pruning into the same representation.

Learnable stochastic gates determine which refinements are active and collectively control each tensor’s precision. Approximate inference over these gates uses priors that favor switching many of them off, encouraging compact solutions. Across several benchmark datasets, the learned pruned networks with mixed precision show a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off than versions with fixed bit widths. These results support jointly learning precision and removal decisions.
neurips-2020-bayesian-bits-unifying-quan.tldr: Bayesian Bits jointly learns pruning and tensor precision through stochastic gates, improving the measured accuracy–efficiency trade-off over fixed-bit networks.

paragraphs: Image classifiers trained on the same dataset can share weaknesses: a small adversarial change that fools one model may also fool another. This transfer makes an ensemble vulnerable when its members fail together. The paper investigates whether separating their weaknesses can improve the ensemble even when individual members remain susceptible to attacks.

DVERGE isolates each member’s adversarial vulnerability by distilling non-robust features, then trains the members to develop different vulnerabilities. Its diversity metric and training procedure aim to produce different outputs when members encounter a transferred adversarial example. The relevant diversity is therefore how models respond to attacks, beyond simply having several models in the ensemble.

The authors report stronger resistance to transfer attacks than previous ensemble methods and further improvements as more members are added. This addresses a weakness they identify in earlier methods, which did not induce enough useful diversity. The findings concern transfer-attack robustness specifically. They support distributing vulnerabilities across an ensemble as an alternative to making every constituent model individually robust through adversarial training.
neurips-2020-dverge-diversifying-vulnera.tldr: DVERGE improves ensemble resistance to transferred adversarial attacks by training its members to have different vulnerabilities.

paragraphs: Many machine learning and statistical procedures depend on eigenvectors, which large problems usually compute through repeated numerical updates. Classical convergence analysis measures the error of an estimated subspace using the spectral norm. The paper asks how convergence behaves under a different measure that better reflects errors across individual entries or rows.

The authors analyze subspace iteration using the ℓ2→∞ norm and derive deterministic convergence bounds. This addresses a gap between recent work on how perturbations affect subspaces and the practical process of actually computing them. Studying the iteration itself makes the analysis relevant to deciding how much numerical work an application needs.

The paper also develops a practical stopping criterion and evaluates it numerically. The reported results show that downstream tasks can achieve comparable performance with fewer iterations, reducing computational time. The significance is that the stopping decision can be informed by a notion of error suited to the application, rather than relying solely on the classical spectral-norm analysis.
neurips-2020-entrywise-convergence-of-it.tldr: Entrywise convergence bounds yield a stopping criterion that can reduce eigenvector iterations while preserving comparable downstream performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a rank-one signal hidden in a symmetric random matrix. Its noise model has independent entries with zero mean and unit variance. With Gaussian noise, the leading eigenvector achieves a well-known optimal statistical threshold, but heavy-tailed noise can make this estimator fail completely.

The authors construct an alternative estimator that reaches the BBP threshold even with heavy-tailed noise. Their finite-size analysis only requires the entry variances to remain constant as the matrix grows. Higher moments may increase arbitrarily quickly or may not exist. This substantially relaxes earlier guarantees that required higher-order moments to stay bounded independently of matrix size.

The estimator is computable in polynomial time by counting self-avoiding walks using a color-coding technique. The authors also extend the construction to spiked tensors and obtain analogous results. The contribution combines statistical robustness under weak moment assumptions with computational feasibility: matching the stated Gaussian-noise threshold does not require the stronger tail restrictions imposed by previous analyses.
neurips-2020-estimating-rank-one-spikes-.tldr: A polynomial-time estimator recovers rank-one signals at the BBP threshold under heavy-tailed noise without bounded higher-moment assumptions.

paragraphs: The Thermodynamic Variational Objective, or TVO, is an inference objective that gives a lower bound on log evidence through one-dimensional numerical integration. Using it requires a sorted set of discretization points, called a schedule. The paper focuses on choosing this schedule, a decision that affects how effectively the objective supports learning and inference.

The authors introduce a Gaussian process bandit method designed specifically to select the integration points. It can automate an initial choice and then move the points as optimization proceeds. This makes the schedule an adaptive part of training, allowing the numerical approximation to change during the learning process rather than remaining fixed throughout.

The paper provides a theoretical guarantee that the bandit procedure converges to the regret-minimizing choice of integration points. Experiments with variational autoencoders and sigmoid belief networks report improved learning and inference. Together, these results support treating the integration schedule as something to optimize dynamically, with both a formal convergence argument and empirical evidence for the proposed selection method.
neurips-2020-gaussian-process-bandit-opt.tldr: A Gaussian process bandit adaptively selects TVO integration points, with convergence guarantees and reported improvements in learning and inference.

paragraphs: Learning with discrete choices often relies on relaxed gradient estimators that make those choices amenable to gradient-based training. The Gumbel-Softmax approach is a familiar example, but extending such methods broadly to large combinatorial distributions remains difficult. Here, a choice can be an entire structured object rather than a single category.

The paper introduces stochastic softmax tricks within the perturbation model framework. These generalize Gumbel-Softmax to combinatorial spaces and provide a common perspective on existing relaxed estimators. The framework also yields new relaxations designed for particular structures, including subsets, spanning trees, and arborescences. Accounting for these structures is central to how the proposed estimators represent the underlying choices.

In comparisons with less structured baselines, the authors find that their methods can train latent-variable models with better performance and greater recovery of latent structure. These are empirical findings about the evaluated models. The broader contribution is a unified way to construct structured relaxations, making combinatorial latent choices more accessible to gradient-based learning.
neurips-2020-gradient-estimation-with-st.tldr: Stochastic softmax tricks generalize Gumbel-Softmax to structured combinatorial choices and improve latent-model learning in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks can perform poorly when training becomes unstable, particularly in text generation. This paper develops a variational training framework motivated by a connection between GANs and reinforcement learning. The connection leads to changes in how both the generator and discriminator are trained.

For the generator, probability-ratio clipping regularizes training to prevent excessively large updates. For the discriminator, sample reweighting reduces the influence of low-quality generated examples. These mechanisms address different parts of the adversarial learning process: the size of generator updates and the contribution of individual fake samples to discriminator training.

The framework also has a theoretical result concerning a known failure mode: in many GANs, an optimal discriminator provides no informative gradient for improving the generator. The authors show that their framework can overcome this issue. When incorporated into several existing GAN architectures, the method significantly improves reported performance on text generation, text style transfer, and image generation. The evidence supports the training approach across these evaluated tasks and architectures.
neurips-2020-improving-gan-training-with.tldr: A variational GAN framework stabilizes learning through generator-update clipping and discriminator sample reweighting, improving several text and image tasks.

paragraphs: In a two-player zero-sum stochastic game, each player learns while facing an opponent who is also changing. This paper studies an episodic setting in which players independently choose policies. Each observes the state and its own actions and rewards, so learning does not rely on a centralized procedure with access to both players’ experience.

The authors prove that when both players use policy gradient methods, their policies converge to a minimax equilibrium under a two-timescale learning-rate rule. The requirement governs how the two players’ update rates relate, and the abstract identifies it as necessary. The convergence claim therefore depends on this specified relationship between learning rates.

The guarantees are global and non-asymptotic, providing finite-sample results rather than only a statement about limiting behavior. The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first such result for independent policy gradient methods in competitive reinforcement learning. It shows that equilibrium learning is possible through independent updates in the studied setting, extending analysis beyond centralized, coordinated computation.
neurips-2020-independent-policy-gradient.tldr: Independent policy gradients have finite-sample convergence guarantees in two-player zero-sum games when their learning rates follow a necessary two-timescale rule.

paragraphs: Exploration is difficult when rewards are sparse and an agent sees only part of its environment. This paper addresses that setting using image observations and a learned world model. The central goal is to estimate what information about the environment is still missing and use that estimate to guide further exploration.

The method first learns representations without external labels, arranging image embeddings according to the temporal distance between observations. The authors find this representation empirically robust to stochasticity and suitable for detecting novelty through a forward model’s prediction errors. The world model operates in this latent representation, while exploration considers uncertainty within an episode and across the agent’s longer experience.

A tabular partially observable labyrinth provides an analysis motivating the approach. The authors then demonstrate it on Atari environments with difficult image-based exploration and report significant improvement over prior work. The findings connect representation learning to exploration: the learned space supports prediction-error signals that can help an agent seek information when external rewards provide little direction.
neurips-2020-latent-world-models-for-int.tldr: A world model in a temporally organized latent space guides exploration through uncertainty and novelty, improving results on hard Atari exploration tasks.

paragraphs: Representing a scene as separate objects can support visual reasoning and control. However, a single image leaves spatial ambiguities about the underlying three-dimensional scene. This paper introduces MulMON, a method that learns object-centered representations by combining several views of a scene containing multiple objects.

A central difficulty is keeping track of which object in one view corresponds to which object in another. MulMON addresses this by iteratively updating latent object representations as it processes multiple views. During training, it must also predict how the scene would appear from new viewpoints. That prediction task encourages the updates to accumulate spatial information across observations.

Experiments show that MulMON resolves spatial ambiguities better than the compared single-view methods and learns more accurate, disentangled object representations. It also predicts object segmentations from novel viewpoints. The results suggest that aggregating views can improve both the internal description of individual objects and the ability to describe their appearance from an unseen perspective.
neurips-2020-learning-object-centric-rep.tldr: MulMON combines multiple views into object-centered scene representations, improving spatial disambiguation and enabling segmentation from new viewpoints.

paragraphs: Discrete graphical models describe joint probability distributions through relationships among variables. Learning them from independent, identically distributed samples can be statistically efficient with the GRISE estimator, yet computationally expensive when the model’s energy function contains higher-order interactions. NeurISE is introduced to address that computational obstacle.

NeurISE places neural network function approximators inside an Interaction Screening objective. Optimizing this objective produces neural representations of conditional distributions. The authors find it a better alternative to GRISE when the true energy function combines high-order interactions with substantial symmetry. In those cases, it discovers compact, correct conditional representations without being supplied prior information about the true model.

The paper also describes training modifications for learning the underlying dependency structure and a variant that represents the full energy function with a neural network. The contribution therefore covers several aspects of model recovery. Its stated advantage is especially relevant to the high-order, highly symmetric setting, where representing interactions through neural functions can alleviate the computational burden of the earlier approach.
neurips-2020-learning-of-discrete-graphi.tldr: NeurISE uses neural networks within Interaction Screening to learn compact graphical-model representations, particularly for high-order interactions with strong symmetry.

paragraphs: Meta-learning trains both a predictive model and a procedure that updates the model from examples of a new task. This creates two places where overfitting can occur. The predictor can fail to generalize, and the learned update procedure can also become too specialized to the tasks encountered during training.

The paper describes these two forms of overfitting and demonstrates them experimentally on common meta-learning benchmarks. It then introduces an information-theoretic framework called meta-augmentation. The framework adds randomness to discourage both components from settling on trivial solutions that work during training but do not transfer well to new tasks.

The authors report large benefits when meta-augmentation is combined with recently proposed meta-regularization techniques. Describing those benefits as complementary means the augmentation contributes alongside those techniques in the reported experiments. The practical lesson is that successful task adaptation depends on generalization at both levels: the predictions a model makes and the procedure it has learned for changing those predictions from new examples.
neurips-2020-meta-learning-requires-meta.tldr: Meta-augmentation adds randomness to address overfitting in both a meta-learned predictor and its update procedure, complementing meta-regularization.

paragraphs: Large pretrained language models can be difficult to fine-tune and serve because of their parameter counts and computation requirements. MiniLM compresses a Transformer by training a smaller student to imitate the self-attention module in the teacher’s final layer. This provides a task-agnostic way to transfer knowledge into the smaller model.

The student learns both the teacher’s attention distributions and relationships expressed by scaled dot-products between value vectors. The latter adds a form of attention-module knowledge beyond the query–key relationships used in existing work. The authors also show that introducing a teacher assistant helps distill large pretrained Transformers.

The monolingual experiments outperform the stated baselines across different student sizes. One reported configuration uses half the teacher’s Transformer parameters and computations while retaining more than 99% of its accuracy on SQuAD 2.0 and several GLUE tasks. That figure describes retained teacher performance, not an absolute accuracy of 99%. The method also obtains competitive multilingual results, supporting its use beyond the evaluated monolingual setting.
neurips-2020-minilm-deep-self-attention-.tldr: MiniLM distills final-layer self-attention relationships into smaller Transformers, retaining over 99% of teacher accuracy on several tasks with half the Transformer resources.

paragraphs: A weighted sampler should choose each item with probability proportional to its assigned weight. Many practical samplers use heuristics without rigorous distribution-quality guarantees, making verification important. An earlier verifier handled uniform sampling, but its techniques did not extend to general weights. This paper introduces Barbarik2 to address that broader problem.

Barbarik2 tests whether a sampler’s output distribution is within an epsilon tolerance of a target distribution or at least an eta distance away. These are separated testing cases, so the result is not a promise to classify every intermediate discrepancy. The method accepts arbitrary weight functions and uses different techniques and analysis from the earlier uniform verifier.

Its sample bound depends on the tolerances and the squared tilt, the largest ratio between two item weights, rather than directly on the number of items as in the cited black-box approaches. This changes what controls verification cost, although weight imbalance still matters. The authors implement a prototype and apply it to three state-of-the-art samplers.
neurips-2020-on-testing-of-samplers-a494.tldr: Barbarik2 tests weighted samplers against arbitrary target distributions with sample complexity governed by weight ratios and testing tolerances.

paragraphs: Epoch-based stochastic gradient descent achieves an optimal convergence rate for strongly convex minimization. This paper asks whether a corresponding method can achieve that rate when minimization and maximization occur together. The setting assumes strong convexity in the minimizing variables and strong concavity in the maximizing variables.

The authors provide a sharp analysis of epoch-wise stochastic gradient descent ascent, called Epoch-GDA. They show an optimal O(1/T) rate for the duality gap after T iterative updates, without additional smoothness assumptions or restrictions such as bilinear structure. The duality gap measures how far the current pair is from resolving both sides of the optimization problem.

The result extends an established minimization guarantee to a more demanding minimax setting through new technical analysis. The authors also reuse a key lemma for weakly convex, strongly concave objectives, obtaining nearly optimal complexity without smoothness or other structural requirements. The main significance is the combination of fast convergence and broad applicability within these explicitly stated convexity and concavity conditions.
neurips-2020-optimal-epoch-stochastic-gr.tldr: Epoch-GDA achieves an optimal O(1/T) duality-gap rate for strongly convex–strongly concave stochastic minimax problems without additional smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can reduce costly exploration by using an oracle policy during training. With several imperfect oracles, however, their advice may conflict and there is no single obvious performance target. This paper proposes comparing the learner against the highest oracle value at each state, giving a benchmark that can draw on different oracles’ strengths.

The authors introduce MAMBA by reducing policy optimization to online learning. Its policy updates use a gradient estimator in the style of generalized advantage estimation. The theoretical analysis establishes that MAMBA can learn a policy competitive with the proposed benchmark and shows how its design enables larger improvements over oracle policies than the imitation-learning state of the art.

The analysis includes the single-oracle case, so the approach is not limited to combining several sources of advice. Experiments compare MAMBA with standard policy gradient using generalized advantage estimation and with AggreVaTe(D). They demonstrate faster policy optimization using demonstrations from either one oracle or multiple weak oracles, supporting the value of learning beyond simple imitation.
neurips-2020-policy-improvement-via-imit.tldr: MAMBA learns from imperfect oracles using their state-wise maximum value as a benchmark, with theoretical guarantees and faster policy optimization in experiments.

paragraphs: Object localization requires a detector to predict where an object is. Regression efficiently predicts continuous quantities, while verification tasks can be easier to infer accurately. This paper combines these strengths in RepPoints, whose localization predictions previously relied heavily on regression. The resulting detector is called RepPoints v2.

The contribution adds verification tasks to the localization process so that the detector uses both methodologies. The motivation is that strong overall detection performance can still leave room to improve the way locations are inferred. Combining verification with regression provides an additional source of supervision for the localization prediction.

On the COCO benchmark, the authors report consistent gains of about 2.0 mAP over the original RepPoints across different backbones and training methods. A single RepPoints v2 model reaches 52.1 mAP on COCO test-dev. They also demonstrate improvements in other detection frameworks and instance segmentation. These results suggest that the combination has usefulness beyond the particular detector where it was introduced.
neurips-2020-reppoints-v2-verification-m.tldr: RepPoints v2 adds verification tasks to regression-based localization, delivering consistent COCO detection gains and benefits in related vision frameworks.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning video representations from visual data without class supervision. It first investigates a supervised contrastive setting and finds that adding positive examples from the same semantic class improves instance-based InfoNCE training. That result motivates finding useful class-related positives through a self-supervised procedure.

The proposed co-training scheme uses two complementary views of the same videos: RGB streams and optical flow. One view identifies positive class samples for training the other. In this way, information available through one representation helps shape the contrastive learning problem faced by the other, extending how positive examples are obtained.

The authors assess the learned representations on action recognition and video retrieval. On both tasks, they report performance that is state-of-the-art or comparable with other self-supervised methods, while requiring substantially less training data to reach similar performance. The reported efficiency benefit therefore concerns data needed for training. The findings support using complementary visual streams to improve the supervision that contrastive learning can generate for itself.
neurips-2020-self-supervised-co-training.tldr: RGB and optical-flow views supply positives for each other’s contrastive training, producing competitive video representations with substantially less training data.

paragraphs: SLIP addresses online prediction in unknown, partially observed linear dynamical systems with stochastic noise. If the system parameters were known, the Kalman filter would be the optimal linear predictor. The challenging case here includes marginally stable systems with long-lasting forecast memory, where existing predictive models can perform poorly.

The authors analyze the complexity of the Kalman filter’s coefficient set through its generalized Kolmogorov width. This motivates a spectral construction that tightly relaxes the Kalman predictive model into a convex learning problem. The resulting algorithm, the spectral LDS improper predictor, runs in polynomial time and is intended to be practical.

A finite-sample analysis gives logarithmic regret against the Kalman filter in hindsight, bounding the accumulated prediction disadvantage. The proof uses Mendelson’s small-ball method and avoids concentration, boundedness, and exponential-forgetting assumptions. Empirical evaluations outperform the compared state-of-the-art LDS predictors. Together, the theory and experiments clarify how efficient prediction can remain possible when observations are incomplete and past information continues to matter for a long time.
neurips-2020-slip-learning-to-predict-in.tldr: SLIP uses a spectral convex relaxation to predict partially observed linear systems with long memory, achieving logarithmic regret against the Kalman filter.

paragraphs: This paper reduces neural network cost by exploiting structure within convolutional building blocks. It introduces Composite Kernel structures, which express convolutions through efficient scaled sum-pooling components. Structured Convolutions are a special case that decomposes an operation into sum-pooling followed by a smaller convolution with fewer weights and lower computational complexity.

The decomposition applies to two-dimensional and three-dimensional kernels as well as fully connected layers. A Structural Regularization loss encourages layers to adopt the required structure during training. This matters because the resulting layers can then be decomposed after training with the reported negligible performance loss, linking the training objective to the intended efficient implementation.

Experiments produce structured ResNets up to twice as small and a more efficient Structured-MobileNetV2 within a 1% accuracy loss on the stated image-classification datasets. The authors also demonstrate structured EfficientNet and HRNet variants. Across their comparisons, complexity reduction matches or exceeds existing tensor-decomposition and channel-pruning methods, supporting the approach across several architectures and vision applications.
neurips-2020-structured-convolutions-for.tldr: Structured Convolutions train layers to support efficient pooling-plus-convolution decompositions, reducing model size and complexity with small reported performance losses.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning often learns an environment model by predicting observed state transitions. This paper argues that limited model capacity may be better spent preserving what value-based planning needs. It introduces value equivalence: two models are equivalent relative to specified functions and policies when they produce identical Bellman updates.

This definition makes model adequacy depend on the planning operations under consideration. The authors formulate model learning around that requirement and analyze how the acceptable model set changes. Adding more policies and functions makes equivalence more restrictive, eventually leaving only a model that fully describes the environment.

For a smaller relevant set, value equivalence may allow simpler models without sacrificing performance, potentially saving computation and memory. Experiments compare this learning approach with traditional alternatives such as maximum likelihood estimation and illustrate its benefits. The authors also argue that the principle helps explain several successful reinforcement-learning architectures. The contribution provides a theoretical way to relate model detail to the specific value computations an agent needs.
neurips-2020-the-value-equivalence-princ.tldr: Value equivalence defines environment models by the Bellman updates they preserve, potentially enabling simpler models suited to an agent’s planning needs.

paragraphs: Causal graph discovery seeks causal relationships from observational data, but the resulting graph can reveal sensitive information about dataset participants. This paper introduces Priv-PC, a differentially private discovery algorithm designed to improve both the usefulness of the recovered graph and the time needed to compute it.

Its central design is a sieve-and-examine procedure. A small portion of the privacy budget filters out queries judged insignificant, leaving more budget for accurate answers to significant queries. The method therefore allocates privacy resources selectively. The paper also provides sensitivity analyses for conditional independence tests, including conditional Kendall’s tau and conditional Spearman’s rho, examining their responsiveness to changes in the data.

The evaluation uses seven public datasets and compares Priv-PC with the state of the art. It reports speedups from 10.61 to 293.87 times alongside better utility. These empirical findings indicate that the proposed allocation procedure can improve both runtime and result quality in the evaluated settings, helping make privacy-preserving graph discovery more practical.
neurips-2020-towards-practical-different.tldr: Priv-PC selectively spends its privacy budget on significant queries, improving causal-graph utility and runtime across seven evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: GAN training is often unstable, and many methods modify models or discrete updates to control that instability. This paper instead examines the continuous-time dynamics underlying training. Its theory and toy experiments suggest those dynamics can be surprisingly stable, motivating a closer look at how numerical updates approximate them.

The authors hypothesize that discretization introduces integration errors responsible for training instability. They investigate established ordinary differential equation solvers, including Runge–Kutta methods, as training procedures. Experiments show that these solvers can stabilize training when combined with a regularizer that controls integration error. The combination is part of the reported result, rather than a claim that any ODE solver alone suffices.

Evaluations on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet outperform several strong baselines. The findings support numerical integration as a useful perspective for designing GAN training methods. They also provide experimental evidence consistent with the proposed explanation of instability, while the broader claim that discretization error causes GAN training instability remains framed as a hypothesis.
neurips-2020-training-generative-adversa.tldr: ODE solvers combined with integration-error regularization stabilize GAN training, supporting the hypothesis that discretization contributes to instability.

paragraphs: Blind super-resolution must recover a sharper image while also estimating the unknown blur that produced the low-resolution input. Earlier approaches train these two steps separately. That separation can create incompatibility: a small blur-estimation error can seriously damage restoration, while estimating blur from the low-resolution image alone provides limited information.

The paper combines a Restorer and an Estimator in one network. The Restorer uses the current blur estimate to reconstruct an image, and the Estimator uses that reconstruction to improve the blur estimate. Repeating and unfolding this alternating process creates an end-to-end trainable system in which each module helps the other.

The Estimator gains access to both low-resolution and restored images. Meanwhile, the Restorer trains with the Estimator’s actual predictions, which could make it more tolerant of estimation errors. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real images report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods, visually preferable outputs, and much higher speed. The results support learning the two coupled tasks together.
neurips-2020-unfolding-the-alternating-o.tldr: An end-to-end network alternates blur estimation and image restoration, improving blind super-resolution quality and speed in the reported experiments.
